timing_rule: Latest eligible year per source within 3 years; dated fieldwork must end before the decision, otherwise an earlier calendar year is required. Retain all eligible question variants in that year.

handgun_bans.support_definition: Original ban-support categories retained separately for possession and sales. Context only; no combined score.

functional_home_firearm.support_definition: No reviewed question about keeping a lawful home firearm usable for self-defense.

cases.name: District of Columbia v. Heller

components.decision: The Court invalidated D.C.’s handgun ban and recognized an individual right to keep a firearm for self-defense at home.
components.scope: The right is not unlimited. This did not invalidate all firearm regulation.
components.survey_fit: Gallup asks about possession generally; Pew asks about sales. Neither isolates D.C.’s home-possession rule or asks whether the Constitution protects it.

observations.wording: Whether handgun possession should be banned, with exceptions for police and other authorized people.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. Dates and percentages come from the historical table in the 2016 report, not its 2016 sample. Historical sample size is not supplied in that table.
observations.weight: Published national topline; no respondent-level recalculation.
observations.denominator: Published full response distribution, including no opinion. Original percentages retained; historical sample size not stated in this table.
observations.orientation: Opposing the ban favors allowing possession; it does not imply opposition to all gun regulation.

observations.wording: Favoring or opposing a ban on handgun sales.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. Nationwide telephone survey of 1,502 adults; asked all respondents. PDF page 5 documents methodology; page 7 (printed page 6) gives Q27. Sales are distinct from possession.
observations.weight: Published national topline; no respondent-level recalculation.
observations.denominator: All 1,502 adults, including don’t know/refused responses. Original percentages retained.
observations.orientation: Favor means favoring the sales ban; oppose means opposing it.

components.issue: Keeping a firearm usable for self-defense
components.decision: The Court also invalidated the requirement that lawful firearms at home remain inoperable when needed for self-defense.
components.scope: This is not a ruling against every safe-storage requirement.
components.survey_fit: Neither selected question addresses storage or immediate usability for self-defense.

cases.interpretation_limit: The judgment was 5–4. The two components concern different rules; broad handgun preferences cannot answer both.

cases.name: McDonald v. City of Chicago

components.issue: Applying the right to state and local governments
components.decision: The Court held that the right recognized in Heller applies against state and local governments, reversing and remanding.
components.scope: The case extended the constitutional protection; it did not resolve every local firearm rule.
components.locator: Alito opinion, Parts III–IV; Thomas concurrence.
components.survey_fit: Earlier opposition to handgun bans provides policy context, not an answer to the constitutional incorporation question. Pew’s 2008 observation is reused background, not a new 2010 measurement.

cases.interpretation_limit: Five justices agreed on the result. Four relied on due process; Thomas used the Privileges or Immunities Clause. General policy preferences do not adjudicate that distinction.

limitations: Explicit source-based legal coding is an input, not an automated legal classifier.
Contextual matches do not measure approval of the specific holding.
Mixed and unresolved components retain their labels; no scalar direction is inferred.
No pooling, confidence intervals, causal claims, or prediction.
